                                  13          On May 5, 2026, the Court held an Order to Show Cause hearing, with Plaintiff’s counsel,

                                  14   Payam Shahian and Larry Chae, and Defendant’s counsel, Glen Olives, present. See Order to

                                  15   Show Cause, ECF No. 66. The Court reviewed the Response to the Order to Show Cause filed by

                                  16   Mr. Shahian earlier the same day. ECF No. 93.

                                  17          As the Court noted on the record, Mr. Shahian’s Response was insufficient, and failed to

                                  18   comply with the Court’s April 22, 2026 Order issued on the record during the previous hearing,

                                  19   which was further memorialized in a April 28, 2026 written Order.

                                  20          The Court maintained the Order to Show Cause, ECF No. 66, with minor amendments.

                                 DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1          I, PAYAM SHAHIAN, declare as follows:

 2          1.      I am an attorney licensed to practice law in California and before this Court. I am

 3   the founder and managing partner of Strategic Legal Practices, APC (“SLP”), counsel of record

 4   for Plaintiff Santiago Talavera Castro. I submit this declaration in response to the Court’s April

 5   28, 2026, Order Imposing Sanctions and Continuing Order to Show Cause as to Plaintiff and

 6   Plaintiff’s Counsel (Dkt. No. 66) (the “April 28 Order”). I make this declaration based on

 7   personal knowledge, and otherwise on information and belief, including based on information

 8   from various orders assembled and reviewed through outside ethics counsel retained by SLP to

 9   assist me in responding to the April 28 Order. If called as a witness, I could and would testify

10   competently to the matters set forth herein.

11          2.      I provide the information set forth in this declaration without waiving, and

12   expressly reserving, the attorney-client privilege, the attorney work-product doctrine, and any

13   other applicable privileges or protections. Nothing in this declaration is intended, and nothing

14   should be construed, as a waiver of any privilege or protection held by SLP, by me, or by any

15   client of SLP. Any communications with, or materials prepared by or at the direction of, outside

16   ethics counsel are submitted only for the limited purpose of responding to the April 28 Order and

17   are not intended to waive any privilege or protection.

18          3.      The April 28 Order requires this declaration to be filed by May 5, 2026, and

19   required my personal in-person appearance on May 6, 2026 (which was subsequently advanced

20   to May 5, 2026 (see Dkt. 74)). The Order was issued on April 28, 2026, and the transcript of the

21   April 22, 2026 hearing—which I did not personally attend—was not made available until on or

22   about the same day the April 28 Order was issued, notwithstanding that Plaintiff’s counsel had

23   ordered the transcript on on April 23, 2026. Plaintiff sought a thirty-day extension by ex parte

24   application. While that application was pending, I have, with the assistance of outside ethics

25   counsel, used the limited time available to prepare this declaration in good faith and to the best

26   of my present ability.

27

28
                                               2
                                 DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1          4.      During the same period in which I have been preparing this declaration, my father

 2   was hospitalized at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, California, requiring my

 3   attention to family matters. In addition, Tionna Carvalho, the only other SLP partner at the time,

 4   departed the firm effective May 1, 2026, and I have been simultaneously occupied with matters

 5   relating to her departure and the transition of firm management. The compressed timing,

 6   combined with these personal and professional circumstances, has materially limited the time

 7   available for the comprehensive investigation that the April 28 Order contemplates. I have

 8   nevertheless attempted, in good faith and through outside ethics counsel, to provide as complete

 9   a response as is reasonably practicable in the time available.

10          5.      Because of the time constraints described above, and the scope of the Court’s

11   request, this declaration is limited to sanctions information from federal courts within the State

12   of California of which I am presently aware after a good-faith inquiry conducted with the

13   assistance of outside ethics counsel. SLP has worked with hundreds of attorneys (including

14   contract attorneys and others) over its sixteen-year history, and historical records concerning that

15   period were maintained in different databases or systems that are no longer available.

16                   Responses to the Specific Items Listed in the April 28 Order

17          6.      Item No. 1: Whether I have ever been personally sanctioned by any court. Based

18   on my personal knowledge and on a review conducted with outside ethics counsel of available

19   federal court records in California, I am not aware of any instance in which any federal court in

20   California has imposed a monetary sanction on me personally. I have never been counsel of

21   record in any of the cases in which sanctions have been imposed on SLP attorneys in a California

22   federal court of which I am presently aware. A chart compiled with the assistance of outside

23   ethics counsel summarizing the federal-court sanction matters identified to date involving SLP

24   attorneys is attached hereto as Exhibit A. Because I have not been personally sanctioned, the

25   chart format requested for Item Nos. 1(a)–(d) is not applicable as to me. I separately address Item

26   No. 4 below.

27

28
                                                3
                                  DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1          7.      Item No. 2: Whether a court has ever imposed non-monetary sanctions (e.g., issue

 2   preclusion or dismissal) against me personally. Based on the same investigation, I am not aware

 3   of any non-monetary sanction (including, without limitation, any issue preclusion or dismissal

 4   sanction) imposed against me personally in any federal court in California. As reflected in Exhibit

 5   A, the only dismissal entered as a sanction in any matter identified involving SLP attorneys was

 6   in Murillo v. FCA US, LLC, No. 22-cv-3970 PA (PDx) (C.D. Cal. May 8, 2023), in which the

 7   case was dismissed without prejudice under Rule 41(b); I was not counsel of record in that matter.

 8   Regardless, the Murillo case settled favorably for the client pursuant to an accepted Rule 68 offer

 9   for $115,000 (with plaintiff’s fees and costs up to the date of the offer, if not resolved between

10   the parties, to be determined by properly noticed motion). (See Murillo, Docket No. 36 (Request

11   for Entry of Judgment and Exhibit A (signed Rule 68 Offer)).

12          8.      Item No. 3: Any instance where a court found that I personally breached

13   professional conduct obligations, irrespective of any sanction. Based on the same investigation,

14   I am not aware of any instance in which any federal court in California has made a finding that I

15   personally breached professional conduct obligations. Exhibit A reflects the findings made by

16   various courts in matters in which SLP attorneys, but not me personally, were counsel of record.

17          9.      Item No. 4: Attestation. Subject to the limitations described in paragraphs 3–5

18   above (including the limitation of this declaration to California federal courts and the time

19   constraints under which it was prepared), I attest that, to the best of my knowledge after the good-

20   faith inquiry described herein, I have not personally been the subject of any sanction by any

21   federal court within the State of California.

22          10.     Item No. 5: Chart of sanctions imposed on attorneys for conduct during their time

23   at SLP. A chart of the California federal court sanctions involving SLP attorneys identified to

24   date is attached as Exhibit A and is incorporated herein by reference. Exhibit A is the product of

25   an independent investigation conducted under the direction of outside ethics counsel; it does not

26   rely solely on, and does not incorporate by reference, the declarations previously filed in this

27   matter by individual SLP attorneys. As noted in paragraph 5 above, the chart is limited to federal

28
                                                4
                                  DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1   courts within the State of California and to the information identified to date through that

 2   investigation.

 3          11.        Item No. 6: Sanctions imposed on SLP. The instances of which I am presently

 4   aware in which a federal court in California has imposed a sanction on SLP as a firm are reflected

 5   in Exhibit A. Outside ethics counsel has been engaged and is continuing to assist with this aspect

 6   of the inquiry.

 7          12.        Item No. 7: State Bar reporting compliance. With respect to State Bar reporting

 8   obligations, the firm provides its attorneys and law clerks with access to The Rutter Group

 9   California Practice Guides for federal and state court practice through Westlaw, and provides full

10   Westlaw access for federal and state legal research, including with respect to professional

11   responsibility obligations. To the extent any sanction reflected in Exhibit A is at or above the

12   $1,000 threshold under Business and Professions Code section 6086.7, the date of any such report

13   and the identity of the reporter, where presently known, are reflected in the chart or are the subject

14   of continuing inquiry by outside ethics counsel.

15          13.        Item No. 8: Steps personally taken to ensure firm-wide compliance. Having

16   reviewed the April 28 Order and other recent orders that have been brought to my attention, I

17   understand that I have additional work to do as the founder and managing partner of SLP, and I

18   am committed to doing it. The steps I have personally taken, and am taking, include the

19   following:

20                a. Following the recent departure of Tionna Carvalho from her prior senior

21                     leadership role and the transition in the firm’s partnership structure, I have

22                     elevated two additional attorneys to partner, Mani Arabi and Larry Chae,

23                     expanding the partnership ranks responsible for supervising matters firm-wide.

24                b. I have become more directly and personally involved in the training of

25                     associates. Effective post-COVID remote-work practices have made hands-on

26                     supervision more difficult, but I have nevertheless committed to a program in

27                     which outside ethics counsel will deliver a monthly seminar to firm attorneys

28
                                                  5
                                    DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1      addressing professional responsibility, court compliance, and related ethical

 2      issues.

 3   c. In addition to the daily meetings I conduct with associates regarding the rules of

 4      civil procedure and case management, I have ensured that The Rutter Group

 5      California Practice Guides for federal and state practice are made available to

 6      every attorney and law clerk at the firm through Westlaw, and that each attorney

 7      has access to Westlaw for legal research, including research concerning

 8      professional responsibility and court rules.

 9   d. SLP is making a significant investment in a new firm-wide case management

10      system, the implementation of which will take several months to complete. The

11      new system is intended to address, among other things, calendaring, deadline

12      tracking, and supervisory review. The firm is also hiring additional attorneys to

13      handle the increased volume of matters arising from the manufacturers’

14      coordinated litigation strategy against SLP. Manufacturers have retained law

15      firms across the United States to litigate Lemon Law cases, and I recognize that

16      more attorneys are needed to meet that landscape; SLP, with its sixteen-year

17      record as a leading firm representing California consumers in Lemon Law

18      matters, is committed to meeting that need while improving compliance and

19      supervision.

20   e. I understand and acknowledge that the trial documents in this case were

21      submitted late, and that significant sanctions were imposed on SLP attorneys as

22      a result of the failures associated with the March 18, 2026 pretrial deadline, in

23      addition to the $500 sanction imposed on the defense firm RoseWaldorf LLP. I

24      take those sanctions seriously and have personally communicated to all firm

25      attorneys the importance of strict adherence to court-imposed deadlines and the

26      consequences of failing to meet them. I respectfully submit that the volume of

27      late filings and other deadline-related issues that the firm is working to address

28
                                     6
                       DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1      represents a work in progress that was not anticipated when manufacturers

 2      began more aggressively litigating consumer warranty cases—including by

 3      substituting in new defense firms, retaining counsel pro hac vice, and deploying

 4      expanded litigation teams. The firm is continuously addressing these issues, and

 5      I note that the resulting volume and pace of litigation has, to some extent, also

 6      affected even well-organized defense firms with substantial attorney resources. I

 7      am also continuing to improve the firm’s internal processes to manage the

 8      increasing volume of removals to federal court, which I expect will increase

 9      further as a result of orders such as the April 28 Order being cited and published

10      on Westlaw. I welcome that challenge, but respectfully submit that fully

11      implementing the firm-wide compliance improvements described above will

12      require additional time.

13   f. Finally, with respect to the Court’s concern regarding the impact of dismissal on

14      clients, I am not commenting on the specific dismissals referenced in the April

15      28 Order, the circumstances of which are distinct from the improper and late

16      filing of joint trial exhibits for which both parties were sanctioned for.

17      I respectfully note, however, that the decision whether and when to dismiss a

18      case is in many circumstances a strategic litigation decision protected by the

19      attorney-client privilege and the work-product doctrine, and I am concerned that

20      the Court’s general directive concerning dismissals—while well-intentioned—

21      can impede and have chilling effect on the attorney-client communications and

22      the attorneys strategic decision-making in particular matters and provide the

23      defense bar to use it to prejudice attorneys and their clients cases which both the

24      Court and I have an interest to protect.

25   g. This is because there are numerous legitimate strategic reasons a case may be

26      dismissed and a different remedy pursued, including, by way of non-exhaustive

27      example: (i) to provide a pre-litigation demand under Civil Code section 1782,

28
                                   7
                     DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN
  1                  which is a statutory prerequisite to seeking damages under the Consumers Legal

 2                  Remedies Act, before refiling on a CLRA theory; (ii) to refile on a different

 3                  factual or legal theory better supported after further investigation (e.g. under

 4                  CLRA) or other consumer-protection statutes; (iii) to address a curable pleading

 5                  or jurisdictional defect; amongst other instances. See Medina v. St. George Auto

 6                  Sales, Inc., 103 Cal. App. 5th 1194 (2024) (“the discovery rule applies to the

 7                  CLRA’s statute of limitations”). CLRA claims may also be asserted independent

 8                  of any direct contractual relationship between the consumer and the

 9                  manufacturer, and they extend to consumers who purchased used vehicles. See

10                  Cal. Civ. Code § 1780(a); McAdams v. Monier, Inc., 182 Cal. App. 4th 174, 186

11                  (2010); Chamberlan v. Ford Motor Co., 369 F. Supp. 2d 1138, 1144 (N.D. Cal.

12                  2005). The CLRA also requires a pre-filing demand letter under Civil Code

13                  section 1782 before damages may be sought, and it is therefore not uncommon

14                  for a CLRA claim to be addressed pre-litigation; the absence of a refiled

15                  complaint following a dismissal does not necessarily mean that no remedy was

16                  pursued or obtained.

17          14.     I respectfully acknowledge the Court’s concerns. I have prepared this declaration

18   in good faith, under significant time pressure, and with the assistance of outside ethics counsel. I

19   will appear in person on May 5, 2026, as ordered.

20          I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America that

21   the foregoing is true and correct.

22          Executed on May 6, 2026, in San Jose, California.

23
                                            ___/s/ Payam Shahian___________________
24                                                 Payam Shahian

                                  DECLARATION OF PAYAM SHAHIAN

Order Re ECF No. 79. The Court is in receipt of Plaintiff's Ex Parte request for an extension of the May 6, 2026 hearing. The Court is amenable to advancing the date or time of the hearing. The Court is unavailable from May 7 -19, therefore, the hearing time can be shifted on May 6 or the hearing can be advanced. The Court orders the parties to meet and confer regarding a stipulated change of the hearing. The parties shall indicate via stipulation by 12 p.m. on Monday, May 4, 2026, whether they prefer to: (a) keep the current date and time; (b) shift the hearing time on May 6, 2026 (any time that day is possible); or (c) advance the hearing to May 5 (the Court is available at any time that day). Should the parties elect to advance the hearing to May 5, Mr. Shahian must bring his declaration as ordered (see ECF No. 74) to the hearing. Signed by Judge Noel Wise on May 1, 2026.
